proposed_node.title: Mitochondrial fusion and fission dynamics
proposed_node.canonical_question: How do mitochondria fuse and divide, and what proteins control this?
proposed_node.summary: Mitochondria constantly fuse and divide to maintain a healthy network. Fusion is driven by MFN1, MFN2, and OPA1; fission is driven by DRP1 recruited by FIS1 and MFF.

sections.heading: A network that constantly reshapes itself
sections.body: Mitochondria are not fixed, isolated blobs. Inside a cell they form a dynamic network that continuously fuses together and pinches apart in a process called mitochondrial dynamics. This reshaping lets cells repair damaged mitochondria, distribute energy evenly, and respond to stress.

sections.heading: Fusion: joining two mitochondria into one
sections.body: When two mitochondria fuse, their outer membranes merge first, then their inner membranes merge. Two proteins called Mitofusin 1 (MFN1) and Mitofusin 2 (MFN2) sit on the outer membrane and physically tether neighbouring mitochondria together and drive outer membrane fusion. A third GTPase called OPA1 sits on the inner membrane and drives inner membrane fusion. All three proteins use GTP hydrolysis as an energy source to pull the membranes together.

sections.heading: Fission: splitting one mitochondrion into two
sections.body: Division is carried out mainly by a cytosolic GTPase called DRP1 (dynamin-related protein 1). DRP1 is recruited from the cytoplasm to the outer mitochondrial membrane by receptor proteins including MFF (mitochondrial fission factor) and FIS1. Once there, DRP1 molecules assemble into a ring-like structure that constricts the outer and inner membranes until the mitochondrion pinches in two.

sections.heading: Why balance between fusion and fission matters
sections.body: Healthy cells maintain a balance between fusion and fission. Excess fission produces many small, fragmented mitochondria. Excess fusion produces an over-connected network. Damaged mitochondria that cannot fuse are targeted for removal by mitophagy, a selective form of autophagy. Disrupting DRP1 or the mitofusins is linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A.

rendering.audience_note: Written for a 16-18 learner at plain-language level with no prior knowledge of mitochondrial dynamics assumed.
